Repeating training data during pretraining usually hurts base-model performance relative to using fresh data, especially when unique data is the bottleneck [1, 2, 3]. The damage is systematic: exact-document repetition can create a worst-case intermediate repeat count, can waste a substantial fraction of compute, and tends to increase memorization while degrading generalization [1]. With finite unique-document pools, the loss penalty is mild for small models but grows quickly for larger models, including for semantically redundant data as models become more capable [3].

How much repetition hurts depends on how it is done [2]. A second epoch is nearly as valuable as a fresh one, but repeated tokens become much less valuable after a critical epoch count; larger models tolerate fewer epochs when the corpus is fixed [2]. Repeat structure also matters: consecutive shard replay and concentrating repeats on fewer samples both raise loss [2]. One exception is diffusion language models: under limited unique data, they can outperform autoregressive models by training for more epochs on repeated data [10].
